The body of `bad` would be instantiated only if `bad` were used, and it is not. questions.prompt: In C++23, which kinds of templates can be partially specialized?
options: Class templates, variable templates and function templates
Class templates, variable templates and alias templates
questions.explanation: Class templates have always allowed partial specialization, and variable templates allow it since they were added in C++14. Function templates cannot be partially specialized: the language expects you to overload them instead, and partial ordering picks the more specialized overload. Alias templates cannot be specialized at all, neither fully nor partially.

`S<int*>` uses the explicit specialization, which is an exact match for those arguments. `S<const int*>` matches the partial specialization `S<T*>` with `T` deduced as `const int`. `S<int* const>` is a const pointer: the top-level `const` is part of the argument type, and `int* const` does not have the form `T*`, so the primary template is used. The tempting first option forgets that matching is on the exact type, cv-qualifiers included.

When the explicit specialization is declared, only `f(T)` exists, so it is a specialization of that template with `T = int*`. Overload resolution then considers only the two primary templates; `f(T*)` is more specialized and wins, and it has no explicit specialization for `int`, so `f(T*)` runs. The tempting answer `f<int*>` is what you get if the specialization is declared after `f(T*)`, because it would then specialize the better template. Explicit specializations never take part in overload resolution themselves.

questions.prompt: According to the C++23 standard, what is the status of this program?
options: Well-formed; `main` returns 1, because only `score(const A&)` is visible where `pick` is called
Well-formed; `main` returns 2, because instantiation happens at the end of the file
Ill-formed: `score` is not declared when `pick` is defined
questions.explanation: `pick<n::A>` has a point of instantiation right after the declaration of `first`, and the end of the translation unit is also a point of instantiation. At the first, argument-dependent lookup finds only `score(const A&)`; at the second it also finds `score(A&)`, a better match for the lvalue `t`. Two points of instantiation that give different meanings make the program ill-formed, no diagnostic required. GCC 16 and Clang 21 both return 2, which is why the second option is tempting, but that is what the implementations happen to do, not a guarantee.

questions.prompt: What does the C++23 standard say about this translation unit?
options: Well-formed; `f` returns 1, since the specialization is found at the end of the file
Ill-formed, no diagnostic required, because the specialization is declared after a use that instantiates `Traits<int>`
questions.explanation: An explicit specialization must be declared before the first use that would cause an implicit instantiation, in every translation unit with such a use; otherwise the program is ill-formed and no diagnostic is required. Here `Traits<int>::id` instantiates the primary template first. GCC and Clang do diagnose this case within one file, with "specialization of 'Traits<int>' after instantiation", but the standard does not require it, and across translation units the same mistake goes unnoticed.

questions.prompt: Several translation units include this header and call `Widget<int>{}.run()`. No translation unit contains `template struct Widget<int>;`. What does the standard say?
options: Well-formed: `extern template` is only a hint, and each translation unit may still instantiate `run`
Ill-formed, no diagnostic required; in practice a link error for `Widget<int>::run()`
Ill-formed: the compiler must diagnose the missing explicit instantiation definition
Well-formed: one of the translation units is chosen to instantiate `run`
questions.explanation: An explicit instantiation declaration suppresses implicit instantiation of the definitions of non-inline members such as `run`. If an entity named by an explicit instantiation declaration is used in a way that would otherwise instantiate it, an explicit instantiation definition must appear somewhere in the program, or the program is ill-formed with no diagnostic required. With GCC 16 this program fails to link with an undefined `Widget<int>::run()`. The hint reading is true only for inline functions, which `run` is not, because it is defined outside the class without `inline`.
